title: The Effect of Teacher Coaching on Instruction and Achievement: A Meta-Analysis of the Causal Evidence esearchgate.net/publication/323344838_The_Effect_of_Teacher_Coaching_on_Instruction_and_Achie
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 12, 2025 — original paper: https://www.r
summary: Barton covers Kraft, Blazar, and Hogan's 2018 meta-analysis pooling 60 causally-designed studies of teacher coaching, finding a large pooled effect on instructional practice (0.49 SD) and a smaller but still significant effect on student achievement (0.18 SD). The authors identify which features separate effective coaching from ineffective coaching: it should be individualized, intensive (at least every couple of weeks), sustained over a semester or year, context-specific to the teacher's own classroom, and focused on deliberate practice of discrete skills. A key caution is that effects shrink considerably when coaching is scaled up from small efficacy trials to large-scale programs, implying that quality is hard to maintain at scale. Barton also flags that coaching's power depends on genuine teacher buy-in and relational trust — something difficult to secure if coaching is mandatory or tied to formal evaluation.
points: Teacher coaching produces a large pooled effect on instructional practice (0.49 SD) across 60 causally-designed studies, with a smaller but real knock-on effect on student achievement (0.18 SD).

Effective coaching has a specific recipe: individualized, intensive (contact at least every couple of weeks), sustained over a semester or year, context-specific to the teacher's own room, and focused on deliberate practice of discrete skills.
Quality and focus of coaching interactions matter more than sheer number of contact hours — dosage alone doesn't predict impact.
Effects shrink substantially when coaching programs scale from small efficacy trials to large-scale rollouts, warning against assuming boutique-program results will hold system-wide.
Coaching only works with genuine teacher buy-in and relational trust — a program that feels mandatory or tied to evaluation undermines the openness coaching depends on.
quotes: Combining results across 60 studies that employ causal research designs, we find pooled effect sizes of 0.49 standard deviations (SD) on instruction and 0.18 SD on achievement.

Effective coaching is characterized by several critical features that teachers should seek out in PD opportunities: it must be individualized (one-on-one), intensive (interactions at least every couple of weeks), sustained (over a semester or year), context-specific (in their own classroom), and focused on deliberate practice of discrete skills.
Teachers should note that large-scale programs show significantly smaller effects than small efficacy trials.
Effective coaching requires substantial teacher buy-in and relational trust, which is challenging to achieve if the program is mandatory or tied to evaluation.

For coaching to be effective, its quality and focus may be more important than the actual number of contact hours (dosage), meaning teachers should prioritise the rigour and relevance of interactions over sheer frequency.
Modest changes in practice are unlikely to result in student impacts.
